newsitem.title: USA: Anti-Castro exiles force Cuban music off airwaves.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Castro exiles force Cuban music off airwaves.

text.p: Four days after a Spanish-language radio station in Miami broke new ground by playing music by Cuban pop stars, anti-Castro exiles have forced it to stop, station staff said on Tuesday.

Advertisers canceled spots in protest and a bomb threat was phoned in to the station, Tropical 98.3 FM, on Monday. "We had the balls to try something new and we had our balls cut off," disc jockey Elmo Lugo told Reuters.

Tropical last week became the first Miami radio station to play modern pop music from the communist-ruled island. Tracks from stars such as Los Van Van, Issac Delgado and Manolin el Medico de Salsa, who are hugely popular in Latin America and Europe, filled its airwaves.

Tropical music director Zummy Oro said the station began spinning the discs because of demand from young listeners, including some who had arrived from Cuba recently and wanted to hear their favorite sounds.
"People were asking for it like crazy," she said.

But anti-Castro Spanish-language radio stations immediately went on the offensive. Callers phoned to denounce Tropical for playing Cuban music. Some even said it was a plot by Cuban President Fidel Castro to divide the exile community.
Silvio Leon, an account executive at Result Advertising, confirmed he pulled the advertisements of several clients. Asked why, he told Reuters: "Because I felt like it."
On Monday, the station was evacuated after receiving a bomb threat. A police search found no bomb but station boss Luis Diaz Albertini, fearing for staff safety, barred playing Cuban discs.
"This is the United States and a democracy but apparently some people in Miami don't feel like that," said Oro, who is originally from Panama.

"What happened yesterday is what happens every day in Cuba. There's the irony," said Lugo, a Puerto Rican. "They are international artists who have no direct relationship to Castro. They are a new generation growing up in that system."

On Tuesday, calls of support came in from many listeners. One man praised Albertini for trying to take a stand against what he said was an intolerant minority. "This has been going on too long," he said.

Right-wing Cuban exiles have a history of hounding artists they deem to be insufficently hostile to Castro. Last month Puerto Rican salsa singer Andy Montanez was banned from the Miami Carnival after he embraced Cuban troubadour Silvio Rodriguez at a festival in San Juan.

The Centro Vasco, a popular restaurant in Little Havana, closed its doors for good in December after it was firebombed when it a booked a show by Rosita Flores and last May protesters scuffled and spat on concert-goers attending the Miami debut of Cuban jazz piano virtuoso Gonzalo Rubalcaba.

Ninoska Perez, spokeswoman for the most powerful exile group, the Cuban American National Foundation, said she believed that Castro agents had made the bomb threat against Tropical to discredit the exile community. "We are not terrorists," she said.

"I am against censorship but I believe advertisers have a right to support what they like. It is offensive to a lot of people. Every time you play a CD by Los Van Van, the money goes to Cuba and is used to support repression," she added.
